title: Open fractures: emergency management
subject: surgery-trauma
setting: Emergency department, orthopaedic and orthoplastic services
summary: IV antibiotics within 1 hour of injury, tetanus prophylaxis, photograph then cover the wound with saline-soaked gauze and an occlusive film, realign and splint with repeated neurovascular checks, and arrange orthoplastic debridement: immediately if highly contaminated or ischaemic, within 12 hours if high-energy, otherwise within 24 hours.

sections.title: Assess
items: Treat any wound near a fracture as an open fracture until proven otherwise; a small inside-out puncture wound still counts.
Follow ATLS priorities first: open fractures are rarely the immediate threat to life, but pelvic and femoral fractures can bleed heavily.

Gustilo-Anderson grade (final grade is assigned at debridement): I wound 1 cm or less and clean; II wound over 1 cm without extensive soft tissue damage; IIIA high-energy injury with adequate soft tissue cover; IIIB periosteal stripping needing flap cover; IIIC arterial injury needing repair.
Document neurovascular status before and after every manipulation or splint, and look for compartment syndrome and arterial injury (pulses, capillary refill, ankle-brachial pressure index).

sections.title: Emergency department
items: Give IV antibiotics as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour of injury; do not wait for theatre (BOAST 2017, NICE NG37).
Handle the wound only to remove gross contamination and to photograph it; do not irrigate or perform mini-washouts in the ED. Cover with saline-soaked gauze and an occlusive film.
Photograph the wound when first exposed and keep the images in the record so it does not need to be uncovered again.
Realign and splint the limb (backslab, or traction splint for femoral shaft fractures), then re-check pulses, capillary refill and sensation.
Control active bleeding with direct pressure or a tourniquet; urgent vascular surgery input for absent pulses or an ischaemic limb.
Give tetanus prophylaxis and adequate IV analgesia.

sections.title: Antibiotics (follow the local network policy)
items: All open fractures: cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g if 120 kg or more) every 8 hours for gram-positive cover.
Gustilo III or heavily contaminated wounds: add gram-negative cover, for example gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV once daily, checking renal function and levels (EAST 2011 practice management guideline).
Farmyard, soil or sewage contamination: add high-dose penicillin (benzylpenicillin 2 to 4 million units, 1.2 to 2.4 g, IV every 4 to 6 hours) for clostridial cover.
Severe beta-lactam allergy: clindamycin 600 to 900 mg IV every 8 hours, plus gram-negative cover as above for type III.
Duration: types I and II, stop 24 hours after wound closure; type III, continue for 72 hours after injury or no more than 24 hours after soft tissue cover, whichever comes first (EAST 2011).

sections.title: Surgery
items: Debridement (wound excision) immediately for highly contaminated wounds (agricultural, aquatic, sewage) or vascular compromise; within 12 hours of injury for high-energy fractures (likely Gustilo IIIA or IIIB); within 24 hours for all other open fractures.
Debridement and fixation should be planned and performed jointly by orthopaedic and plastic surgery consultants (orthoplastic care); extend wounds along fasciotomy lines.
Definitive soft tissue closure or cover within 72 hours of injury if not achieved at the first debridement. Internal fixation only when definitive soft tissue cover can follow immediately.
If delayed primary amputation is chosen after multidisciplinary discussion with the patient and family, perform it within 72 hours of injury.
Refer or transfer open fractures of long bones, hindfoot or midfoot to a centre able to provide orthoplastic care.

sections.title: Tetanus prophylaxis
items: Open fractures are tetanus-prone wounds. Give Td (tetanus and diphtheria toxoid) 0.5 mL IM if immunisation is incomplete, unknown, or the last dose was more than 5 years ago.
Also give human tetanus immunoglobulin 250 IU IM at a different site if immunisation is incomplete or unknown.
Complete the primary Td series later in patients who were never fully immunised.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Delaying the first antibiotic dose until the patient reaches theatre.
Repeatedly uncovering the wound for each new examiner instead of using a photograph.
Irrigating or probing the wound in the ED.
Missing compartment syndrome, which can occur despite an open wound.
Primary closure of a contaminated wound, or prolonged antibiotic courses that select resistant organisms.

drugs.name: Cefazolin
drugs.dose: 2 g IV every 8 hours (3 g if 120 kg or more)
drugs.notes: First dose within 1 hour of injury.

drugs.name: Gentamicin
drugs.notes: Add for Gustilo III or heavy contamination; monitor creatinine and levels; use adjusted weight in obesity.

drugs.name: Benzylpenicillin
drugs.dose: 2 to 4 million units (1.2 to 2.4 g) IV every 4 to 6 hours
drugs.notes: Add for farmyard, soil or sewage contamination (clostridial risk).

drugs.name: Td vaccine
drugs.notes: If immunisation incomplete, unknown, or last dose more than 5 years ago.

drugs.name: Human tetanus immunoglobulin
drugs.dose: 250 IU IM at a separate site
